analysis.one_liner: Extends the nuclear industry's accident liability backstop, eases reactor licensing rules, and lifts foreign-ownership limits.
analysis.headline: This nuclear industry licensing bill died in a Senate committee without a hearing or vote, so existing nuclear liability and environmental review rules stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have reauthorized the Price-Anderson system, which caps how much nuclear plant owners must pay after a reactor accident and leaves taxpayers covering costs above that cap, through 2012. It would have repealed the ban on foreign ownership of nuclear licenses, removed antitrust review of license applications, and barred regulators from weighing whether a reactor is needed or whether alternatives exist when doing environmental reviews. It also contained smaller provisions to help the Nuclear Regulatory Commission keep skilled staff and to oversee decommissioning funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear plant owners and prospective reactor builders gain the most: their accident liability stays capped with a taxpayer backstop, antitrust review of their licenses disappears, environmental reviews get narrower, and licensing hearings become less formal. Foreign companies gain the right to own US nuclear licenses. Retired NRC experts rehired as consultants could keep their pensions, and a small training program funds nuclear safety skills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nuclear plant owners and reactor builders

how_it_helps.text: Reauthorizes Price-Anderson mandatory indemnification of nuclear licensees from August 1, 2002 to August 1, 2012, keeping the capped-liability regime that plant operators rely on to insure against accidents.
Repeals the prohibition on foreign ownership of commercial, medical therapy, and research and development nuclear licenses issued by the NRC.
Eliminates antitrust review of NRC license applications, leaving only the agency's own license conditions subject to reconsideration.
Bars the NRC from considering the need for a facility or any alternative to it in environmental reviews of license applications or renewals, narrowing the scope of NEPA review for reactors.
Directs licensing hearings to use informal adjudicatory procedures unless the commission finds formal procedures necessary, reducing the record and process available to intervenors.

Authorizes a training and fellowship program for critical nuclear safety skills, funded at $1 million per year for fiscal 2002 through 2005, and lets the NRC waive the pension offset for retired employees rehired as consultants.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the residual cost of a major nuclear accident beyond the industry's capped liability. People living near proposed reactor sites lose the consideration of energy need and alternatives in environmental reviews, and members of the public have less access to formal hearings challenging licenses. Antitrust review of who may hold nuclear licenses is eliminated entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near reactor sites

drawbacks.text: Extending the Price-Anderson liability cap keeps the public on the hook for accident costs above the industry's insurance and assessment levels, a subsidy the bill's supporters would have to defend each decade.
Prohibiting any consideration of the need for or alternatives to a licensed facility strips a core question out of environmental review for reactor siting.

Eliminating antitrust review of license applications removes an existing check on concentration of nuclear ownership, and the repeal of the requirement for NRC conflict-of-interest rules on contracts, plus allowing national laboratory contracts despite unavoidable conflicts, weakens ethics safeguards at the regulator itself.
Shifting licensing hearings to informal procedures limits the ability of states, tribes, and local groups to build a full record challenging a license.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a few genuine public-interest items — a decommissioning fund oversight provision, a safety-skills training program, and a fix for hiring scarce NRC expertise — with a large package of industry-favoring changes: longer liability indemnification, no antitrust review, no environmental consideration of need or alternatives, looser hearings, and open foreign ownership. The regulatory rollbacks dwarf the public protections, and the 'safety' framing in the title covers mostly promotion of the industry. An honest supporter would have to concede that accident liability beyond the cap falls on taxpayers and that the environmental and antitrust changes remove real checks.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator George Voinovich introduced the bill on October 30, 2001 with original cosponsors Mary Landrieu, Bob Smith of New Hampshire, and James Inhofe, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted, so the bill died at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.

Because it never became law, the Price-Anderson liability reauthorization, the foreign-ownership repeal, the antitrust review elimination, and the narrowed environmental review all failed to take effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, the existing nuclear liability caps, foreign-ownership limits, antitrust review, and full environmental review of reactor licenses all remained in place. The nuclear industry did not get the loosened licensing regime it sought, and taxpayers and communities near reactor sites kept the existing protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and communities near reactor sites

industries.industry: Nuclear power plant owners and prospective reactor builders
industries.note: The bill would have extended the Price-Anderson taxpayer-backed liability regime to 2012, eliminated antitrust review of their licenses, narrowed environmental reviews, and made hearings informal. These changes shift accident costs beyond the insurance cap to taxpayers and reduce public checks on licensing.

Repealing the ban on foreign ownership of NRC-issued licenses would have opened the US commercial, medical, and research nuclear sectors to foreign control, removing an existing national security-linked restriction.

industries.industry: National laboratories and nuclear engineering contractors
industries.note: The bill would have let the NRC contract with national laboratories despite unavoidable conflicts of interest, in exchange for mitigation steps, and would have repealed the requirement for NRC conflict-of-interest rules on contracts. It also funded a small training and fellowship program for nuclear safety skills.

The bill would have given the NRC authority to set standards and restrictions on how former licensees control and disburse decommissioning funds, protecting the money set aside to dismantle retired reactors.
